\title{A Fitted Generative Model of Drone Ego-Noise for Rotor-Speed
  Estimation}

\author{Dmitrii~Mukhutdinov and Lin~Wang%
  \thanks{The authors are with the School of Electronic Engineering and
    Computer Science, Queen Mary University of London, UK (e-mail:
    d.mukhutdinov@qmul.ac.uk; lin.wang@qmul.ac.uk).}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Estimating the four motor speeds of a quadrotor from its own noise is
limited by data: the public annotated flight recordings amount to a few
minutes from two airframes, and models trained on them recognize
trajectories they have already heard instead of reading the harmonic
comb. We replace the data with a model. We fit a probabilistic
generative model of drone ego-noise in two halves, both estimated from
real flights by exact likelihood. The first is a state-space model of
the four rotor-speed trajectories, with a slow and a resonant mode per
control axis, a per-rotor measurement process and a per-flight offset,
fitted to seven rigs; a diagonal Gaussian over a dimensionless
reparametrization of its 32 parameters samples unseen airframes. The
second is a model of the rotor-noise audio given a speed trajectory:
harmonic lines whose phase carries an integrated Ornstein--Uhlenbeck
shaft error and a per-line Lorentzian width, a per-order power profile,
a coloured floor with speed laws, and per-microphone gains, fitted by a
composite Whittle likelihood on bench recordings and then in flight.
We validate the fits with a tracker-parity gate: a frozen estimator
trained on real audio reads the rendered audio at
1.82\revps{} on the DREGON rig against a 2.19\revps{} bar and
1.62\revps{} on the Matrice 100 against 3.03. We then train
rotor-speed estimators on renders alone and on mixtures with real
audio, and report what transfers.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Rotor speed estimation, drone ego-noise, generative models, Whittle
likelihood, state-space models, synthetic training data, sim-to-real
transfer.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\IEEEPARstart{A}{udio} recorded on board a drone could support voice
interaction, acoustic monitoring and self-diagnostics. The main
obstacle is the ego-noise of the rotors, which buries other sources at
signal-to-noise ratios between 0 and $-30$ dB. This noise has a clear
structure: each rotor produces a comb of harmonics spaced by its
rotation rate, plus broadband aerodynamic noise. If the motor speeds
are known, the harmonics can be located, and Gulli et al.
\cite{gulli2025rotorcond} use motor-speed telemetry explicitly to
condition speech-enhancement models. Estimating the speeds from the
audio itself would remove the need for telemetry at inference time.
Flight-controller logs are not always exposed, they have to be aligned
with the audio, and they carry timing and value errors that matter at
harmonic precision (Section~\ref{sec:data}).

The obstacle to estimating the speeds is the annotation. The public
recordings with usable telemetry amount to about seven minutes of
powered flight from two airframes (Section~\ref{sec:data}), which is a
few dozen distinct speed trajectories. A model trained on that much
data can reach a low validation error and still be reading the wrong
cue. We showed previously that it is: a frequency-scaling probe, which
resamples a cruise clip and asks whether the prediction follows the
harmonics, returns a slope near zero for every regressor trained on
real audio alone, and the same models fail by an octave on an unseen
drone. The cue they use is the trajectory prior of the recordings they
saw. More annotated flight is the obvious remedy and it is expensive:
every minute needs an airframe, a flight, a synchronized array and a
telemetry log that survives the alignment.

The contribution of this paper is a fitted probabilistic generative
model of drone ego-noise that supplies the missing data. It has two
halves, and both are estimated from real recordings rather than
designed by hand. The first (Section~\ref{sec:traj}) is a continuous
state-space model of the four rotor-speed trajectories: a slow
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck mode and a damped oscillator per control axis, a
coloured per-rotor measurement process, and a per-flight offset,
fitted to seven rigs by an exact Kalman likelihood and judged against
the best fit of the synthesizer it replaces. The second
(Section~\ref{sec:noise}) is a model of the rotor-noise audio given a
speed trajectory: each order of each rotor is a line whose phase
carries the integrated shaft-speed error shared by all its orders and
an independent Wiener term that gives the line a Lorentzian width;
the line powers form a per-order profile; the broadband floor is a
Gaussian-process-shaped spectrum with its own speed law; and every
microphone has its own line and floor gains. It is fitted by a
composite Whittle likelihood on static bench recordings and then in
flight with the dynamics frozen (Section~\ref{sec:fit}). We validate
the fits against a frozen estimator trained on real audio, a spectral
proxy and the likelihood of a speed-matched oracle
(Section~\ref{sec:fitval}), and we sample rigs from the fits in three
ways of increasing difficulty (Section~\ref{sec:rigs}). The secondary
contribution is the estimator side: compact regressors with a
permutation-invariant loss, and multi-pitch salience architectures
from music transcription equipped with a per-rotor output
representation that makes them competitive (Section~\ref{sec:est}).

Section~\ref{sec:exp} is the experiment that the model exists for. We
train the estimators on renders alone, on renders mixed with the real
pool, and on a curriculum, and we score everything on the same frozen
real validation protocol against real-only references. Every training
stream in this paper is synthetic or mixed; the validation protocol
never changes.

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Drone ego-noise}
Existing approaches to drone ego-noise
reduction include multichannel blind source separation
\cite{wang2020bss}, learned time--frequency masks for single- and
multichannel processing \cite{wang2020dnntf}, and single-channel
band-split attention \cite{liu2025edgebsrof}. These methods use the
microphone signals only. Gulli et al. \cite{gulli2025rotorcond}
condition the enhancement model on the rotor speeds taken from
telemetry. In this work we estimate those speeds from the recorded
sound, and we build the training data for that estimator.

\subsection{Pitch estimation and transcription}
Multi-pitch estimators
predict several simultaneous fundamental frequencies. Neural methods
often output a \emph{salience map}, a time--frequency array whose
values indicate candidate-pitch activity
\cite{bittner2017deepsalience,cuesta2020multif0,bittner2022basicpitch}.
Harmonic convolutions on a log-frequency axis have been used for piano
transcription \cite{wei2022hppnet} and monophonic pitch estimation
\cite{wei2022harmof0}. Our task is different, and we adapt these
architectures to four rotor-speed tracks. At cruise the rotor rates
lie within one octave (55--110\revps) and can be less than 1\revps{}
apart, so the main difficulty is to separate nearby combs.

\subsection{Order tracking}
An \emph{order} is a frequency component
indexed by a multiple of the shaft speed. Tacholess order tracking
estimates the speed from vibration or sound instead of a tachometer
\cite{peeters2019tacholess}, either by time--frequency ridge extraction
\cite{iatsenko2016ridges} or by iterative adaptive Vold--Kalman
filtering, which updates the frequency estimate and the filter
bandwidth together \cite{jiang2024iavkf}. The drone case adds four
simultaneous shafts with near-equal speeds and changes of flight regime
(idle, ramps, cruise, landing). The blind tracker of
Appendix~\ref{sec:tracker} builds on these methods.

\subsection{Synthetic training data and sim-to-real transfer}
Training on simulated data and testing on real measurements is a
standard answer to annotation scarcity, and its failure mode is
well documented. In robotics, \emph{domain randomization} trains on
simulated images whose nuisance parameters are sampled from wide
distributions, so that the real world is one draw among many
\cite{tobin2017domainrand}; randomizing the \emph{dynamics} rather
than the appearance transfers a control policy to hardware
\cite{peng2018dynrand}. The same two ideas appear in audio. Sound
event detection is trained on soundscapes synthesized from isolated
events and backgrounds, which gives strong labels that human
annotation cannot \cite{turpault2019dcase}; end-to-end diarization is
trained on simulated conversations whose statistics are fitted to
real meetings, and the fidelity of those statistics is what decides
the transfer \cite{landini2022simconv}; far-field recognition uses
simulated room impulse responses, whose mismatch against measured ones
is large enough that it is worth learning a correction
\cite{ratnarajah2021tsrir}. In rotating machinery, a numerical model
identified from measurements supplies the labelled fault data that
the real machine cannot \cite{kumar2025numerical}.

Our setting differs from all of these in one respect that shapes the
paper. The quantity we predict, the rotor speed, is the
\emph{input} to the generator, so a render is labelled exactly, with
no annotation error and no alignment; and the generator is not a
physical simulation but a probabilistic model fitted to the same
recordings we validate on. That makes the fidelity of the fit
measurable rather than assumed, and Section~\ref{sec:fitval} measures
it.

\section{Real data, splits and ground truth}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Task}
Given a mono or multichannel recording from a
drone-mounted array, we predict four motor speeds in revolutions per
second (rev/s) on the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) frame grid:
2048-sample windows and a 512-sample hop at 16 kHz, i.e. 31.25
frames/s. We do not assign the estimates to physical rotor identities.
For each frame, we match the four predictions to the four reference
speeds in the order that minimizes the error, both in training
(Section~\ref{sec:est}) and in evaluation, where we report the
matched mean absolute error (MAE). A speed error of 1\revps{} shifts
the fortieth harmonic by 40 Hz, so sub-rev/s accuracy matters for
harmonic-informed suppression.

\subsection{Recordings and splits}
Table~\ref{tab:data} lists all the
recordings we use. DREGON \cite{strauss2018dregon} provides an
8-microphone array mounted under a MikroKopter quadrotor in indoor
free flight, with logged commanded speeds and, for the room-1
recordings, measured speeds from the motor controllers. The second
collection, MD2, contains outdoor flights of a DJI Matrice 100 with an
8-microphone ring and telemetry obtained through the manufacturer's
SDK \cite{clayton2023embedded}. The real training pool consists of the
five DREGON room-2 recordings and one MD2 flight (FLY125): 444 s of
audio, or about one hour of single-channel material if the eight
microphones are counted separately. It contains only a few dozen
distinct speed trajectories, since additional microphones do not
create new trajectories. That scarcity is the premise of this paper.
The validation split consists of 37 fixed 8-second clips
from three DREGON room-1 recordings (22 clips) and a different MD2
flight, FLY124 (15 clips), each with eight channels. This gives
74\,296 scored frames, of which 12.5\,\% are stopped-rotor frames,
3.7\,\% have a rotor between 0.5 and 30\revps{} (take-off and landing
transients), 13.5\,\% are ramps and 70.3\,\% are cruise. Fourteen of
the DREGON clips come from flights with a loudspeaker playing speech
or white noise in the room; the other 23 clips contain rotor noise
only. We hold out two DREGON source flights and two mono MD2 flights
and do not use them in this paper. Every number we report is a
validation number, and we select checkpoints on the same split.

Two of these recordings appear again as fitting data. The DREGON
room-2 recordings and FLY125 are the flights on which the noise model
of Section~\ref{sec:noise} is fitted, and the DREGON and MD2 telemetry
logs are two of the seven rigs of Section~\ref{sec:traj}. The
validation clips are not fitted on.

\subsection{Speech mixing}
During training we mix every 1-s chunk of rotor noise
with a LibriSpeech \cite{panayotov2015librispeech} utterance drawn from
train-clean-100 (100 h, 251 speakers) at a signal-to-noise ratio drawn
uniformly from $[-30, 0]$ dB. The noise is the reference level, with a
floor on the reference so that a silent chunk cannot be scaled into
loud speech. One sixth of the chunks form a zero-labelled ``silence''
arm, which contains speech and room noise but no rotor noise. Without
this arm the models learn that quiet means stopped, and they fail on
silence that carries sound. Each epoch therefore sees fresh mixtures.

\subsection{Ground truth}
The logs are imperfect in ways that matter at
harmonic precision. We made three decisions about them.
(i) The DREGON labels are the \emph{commanded} speed after a cleaning
step: we zero the leading constant segment before the motors respond
and median-filter single-sample spikes. The commanded track freezes at
its last value when the controller stops logging, so we do not trust it
through shutdown. Measured speeds exist only for the room-1
recordings, from a period-counting tachometer with a 49.7 Hz update
rate and a 0.27\revps{} quantization step at 80\revps{}. They agree
with the cleaned command to 0.04\,\% on average (0.11\,\% in the worst
case), so we use the command for the frozen split as well. (ii)
Compared with the audio itself, the DREGON telemetry over-reports the
speed by 0.35--0.85\,\% depending on the estimator (a
harmonic-residual fit gives 0.54\,\%, with a confidence interval of
0.45--0.62\,\%). No independent measurement decides between the
candidate corrections, so we keep the DREGON labels as logged and
carry the range as an uncertainty floor of 0.3--0.7\revps{} at cruise
under every DREGON number in this paper. (iii) The MD2 SDK log lags
the audio, and the lag grows linearly with time, which indicates a
sample-clock dilation. A fixed lag leaves a 12--16 ms RMS timing
residual, while a lag-plus-slope fit (+0.65 and +0.38 ms per second
for FLY124 and FLY125) leaves 3--5 ms. The logged speeds are also about 0.7\,\% low, so we apply a
multiplicative correction ($\times 1.0070$). The correction has to be
multiplicative because it must vanish at zero speed. We estimate both corrections from the harmonic
reconstruction residual, i.e. we fit a harmonic model to the audio at
a candidate trajectory and measure the energy it leaves, and we apply
them to the training and validation labels alike. An audio-refined
annotation obtained by minimizing that residual starting from the
telemetry has a precision floor of about 0.2\revps{}. We use it as a
fitting target where stated, not as a training or validation label.

\section{The generative model}
\label{sec:model}

The model has two halves. The first is a law for the four rotor-speed
trajectories; the second is a law for the microphone signals given
those trajectories. They are fitted on different data, by different
likelihoods, and they compose: a draw from the first is the input of
the second, and the draw is the label of the render.

We fix the notation for the whole paper here. A quadrotor has rotors
$i = 1,\ldots,4$; a rotor emits orders $k = 1,\ldots,K_i$, the
multiples of its shaft rate below the analysis Nyquist; the array has
microphones $m = 1,\ldots,M$. The speed of rotor $i$ at time $t$ is
$r_i(t)$ in rev/s and $\mathbf r(t)$ is the vector of the four. A
\emph{rig} is one parameter vector of each half: one trajectory law
and one rotor-noise law, together describing one aircraft with one
flight-controller tune.

\todo{Fig.~1: schematic of the two halves --- trajectory state space
  $\to$ $\mathbf r(t)$ $\to$ line/floor synthesis $\to$ 8-channel
  audio, with the fitted blocks marked.}

\subsection{Rotor-speed trajectories}
\label{sec:traj}

\subsubsection{Corpus and support}
We collected telemetry from seven
quadrotor rigs, of which the DREGON MikroKopter and the MD2 Matrice
100 of Table~\ref{tab:data} are two; the other five are public flight
datasets with logged motor speeds. Every log is resampled to a common
100 Hz grid. Only \emph{airborne} samples are used, by a rule that is
frozen and never tuned per rig: with $\bar r(t)$ the mean over rotors,
the threshold is half the 90th percentile of $\bar r$, a sample is
airborne when every rotor exceeds it, and each resulting run is eroded
by 1.0 s at both ends and kept only if 5.0 s survive.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The frozen judge"

\subsubsection{The model}
Write $\mathbf M$ for the quadrotor mixer,
whose columns are the common, roll, pitch and yaw axes, and
$\mathbf R(\beta)$ for a rotation of the (common, yaw) plane that is
the identity on roll and pitch. The trajectory is
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf r(t) = \boldsymbol\mu + \boldsymbol\delta
    + \mathbf M\,\mathbf R(\beta)\,\mathbf v(t) + \mathbf e(t),
  \label{eq:traj}
\end{equation}
with one \emph{mode} process $v_j$ per control axis,
\begin{equation}
  v_j(t) = \mathrm{OU}(\tau_{\mathrm s,j}, \sigma_{\mathrm s,j})
    + \mathrm{CAR}_2(f_{0,j}, \zeta_j, \sigma_{\mathrm o,j}).
  \label{eq:mode}
\end{equation}
$\mathrm{OU}$ is a stationary Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process with time
constant $\tau_{\mathrm s}$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm
s}$, and $\mathrm{CAR}_2$ is the white-noise-driven damped oscillator
$\ddot x + 2\zeta\omega_0\dot x + \omega_0^2 x = \xi$,
$\omega_0 = 2\pi f_0$, with stationary standard deviation
$\sigma_{\mathrm o}$. The oscillator is what makes the pair sufficient:
its spectrum is flat below $f_0$ and falls as $f^{-4}$ above, whereas
a sum of Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes is capped at $f^{-2}$, which
the measured spectra exclude. With $\zeta$ free it is also the
per-rig resonance: $\zeta < 1/\sqrt2$ peaks at $f_0$ (the
MikroKopter's 3 Hz control loop), $\zeta \approx 1$ is a shoulder,
$\zeta > 1$ is the featureless power law of the Matrice 100.
The rotation $\mathbf R(\beta)$ is needed because the two loud modes
are a collective/yaw mixture rather than either axis alone.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The model"

$\mathbf e(t)$ is the \emph{measurement} process: one
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process per rotor with shared
$(\tau_{\mathrm e}, \sigma_{\mathrm e})$, independent across rotors.
The artefacts it absorbs are coloured and incoherent --- the DREGON
log is a 45 Hz sample-and-hold quantized to 0.30\revps{}, the MD2 log
is a 17 Hz asynchronous update resampled at 29.41 Hz with no
anti-alias filter --- so a white term cannot take them, and without
this term the shaft modes take them instead: the DREGON inter-rotor
correlation then comes out at 0.46 against a real 0.17. $\tau_{\mathrm
e}$ is bounded to $(10^{-3}, 1)$ s, the range of the hold times it
models (median hold 68 ms on MD2, 19 ms on DREGON). Labelling the
term ``measurement'' is what lets a training sampler switch it off and
keep the shaft: a stream that renders audio \emph{from} the labels
must not render a logger's staircase as sound.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The model"

$\boldsymbol\delta = \mathbf 1\,\delta_{\mathrm c} + \boldsymbol\delta_{\mathrm r}$
is one draw per flight, with
$\delta_{\mathrm c} \sim N(0, s_{\mathrm c}^2)$ common to the four
rotors and $\boldsymbol\delta_{\mathrm r} \sim N(0, \mathrm{diag}(s_{\mathrm
r}^2))$ per rotor. Between-flight level differences are real and
large: two of the seven rigs differ by about 41\revps{} on all four
rotors at once between a gentle and an aggressive flight, while on the
MD2 rig one rotor's own trim moves 17\revps{}. Finally the sampler
clamps its output to the rig's measured airborne extremes, because a
real ESC has a floor and a ceiling and a Gaussian model does not know
that.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The model"

The parameter vector has 32 entries: $\boldsymbol\mu$ (4), $\beta$,
five per mode ($\tau_{\mathrm s}, \sigma_{\mathrm s}, f_0, \zeta,
\sigma_{\mathrm o}$) for 20, the two measurement parameters, and the
five offset scales. $\boldsymbol\mu$, $s_{\mathrm c}$ and
$\mathbf s_{\mathrm r}$ are moment-estimated from the airborne samples
and never enter the likelihood, so the optimiser sees 23 dimensions;
the state is 16-dimensional (four slow processes, four oscillator
pairs, four measurement processes).
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "Parameters"

\subsubsection{Fitting}
Both shaft components and the measurement
process are defined by their exact discrete state space on the fit
grid, $\mathbf F = \exp(\mathbf A\,\Delta t)$ and
$\mathbf Q = \mathbf P - \mathbf F \mathbf P \mathbf F^{\!\top}$ with
$\mathbf P$ the continuous stationary covariance, so the sampler, the
likelihood and the reported spectrum cannot drift apart. The
continuous-time Lorentzian formula is not used: on a 100 Hz grid it
misses the power folded down from above Nyquist (74\,\% low at 39.5 Hz
for $\tau = 0.3$ s), which an earlier fit paid for by inflating the
measurement term.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "One object, not three"

The likelihood is exact. Each airborne segment is cut into 30 s blocks
overlapping 5 s on the left; the innovations of those burn-in samples
are excluded, so every scored innovation comes from a filter that has
forgotten its initial condition, and a block must contribute at least
5 s of scored samples. All blocks of one padded length are driven
through one batched steady-state recursion
$\mathbf x_{t+1} = (\mathbf F - \mathbf K \mathbf H)\mathbf x_t +
\mathbf K \mathbf y_t$, with the gain $\mathbf K$ and innovation
covariance $\mathbf S$ from the discrete Riccati fixed point iterated
in an autodiff framework, so the gain is differentiable in the
parameters, and
$\mathrm{NLL} = \tfrac12\sum_t [\log\det\mathbf S + \mathbf
e_t^{\!\top}\mathbf S^{-1}\mathbf e_t]$. Each block is demeaned per
rotor, which is why $\boldsymbol\mu$ and the offsets are estimated
rather than fitted. Each rig is fitted at the rate at which its
telemetry is believable rather than on a common grid: the MD2 log is
fitted at 25 Hz, below the interpolation null of its 29.41 Hz update,
and every other rig at 100 Hz. The fit is MAP under log-normal priors
on $\tau_{\mathrm s}$ (median 2.0 s, log-sd 1.5), every $\sigma$
(1.0\revps, 3.0), $\tau_{\mathrm e}$ (0.05 s, 2.0) and
$\sigma_{\mathrm e}$ (0.1\revps, 3.0), maximized by L-BFGS-B on the
analytic gradient with four restarts.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The likelihood is EXACT", "Optimiser"

\subsubsection{The judge and the baseline}
A generative model cannot
be scored by its own likelihood against a different model class, so
the campaign fixed a judge before it started. A trajectory, real or
sampled, is summarised by five statistics, all computed on the same
100 Hz airborne support: the mean speed over all samples
(\textsf{overall\_mean}, discrepancy in rev/s), the same per rotor
(\textsf{rotor\_mean}, RMS over rotors), the per-rotor variance pooled
over flights about the pooled mean (\textsf{rotor\_var}, RMS of
$|\log$ ratio$|$), the biased normalised autocorrelation at 24
log-spaced lags from 0.05 to 10 s (\textsf{acf}, RMS over rotors and
lags), and the zero-lag correlation between rotors (\textsf{xcorr},
RMS over the six pairs). A candidate \emph{passes} a rig only if no
family regresses and at least three improve strictly, which is what
stops a model from trading autocorrelation for variance and calling it
progress. Model statistics are estimated by drawing the real flight
durations 40 times over with antithetic per-flight offsets, so the
offset term contributes no Monte-Carlo error to the pooled mean.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The frozen judge"

The comparison is against the synthesizer the model replaces ---
Poisson-gated rectangular pulses through a first-order lag plus
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck jitter --- fitted per rig at its best rather than
at its defaults. It has no tractable likelihood, so its 22 free
parameters are fitted by simulated moment matching on the same frozen
statistics, by Powell with 300 evaluations under common random
numbers. The fit is not a straw man: where it can, it converts rare
pulses into continuous jitter, driving the maneuver rate and amplitude
to their bounds while the cruise jitter grows tenfold, which is the
incumbent admitting that the real series is continuous wander.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "The baseline the judge compares against"

Table~\ref{tab:traj} is the result. One rig passes all five families
and three more miss by one. The families the incumbent cannot reach
are the ones the new model wins: pooled per-rotor variance improves on
five of the seven rigs and inter-rotor correlation on six, and the
three misses there are small (0.004, 0.038 and 0.024 in the respective
units). What the model does not yet reach is the mean families on the
three rigs with large between-flight level differences. The mechanism
is named: on \textsf{neurobem\_quad} a per-rotor offset of about
41\revps{} on all four rotors manufactures rotor spreads no real
flight has, and the frozen airborne rule then drops those samples from
the low side only, keeping 68.6\,\% of them. Splitting the offset into
a common and a per-rotor part fixes exactly that rig (retention
$0.686 \to 0.873$, \textsf{overall\_mean} $3.65 \to 1.11$,
\textsf{rotor\_var} $0.139 \to 0.064$) and breaks the one whose offset
is genuinely one rotor's trim: \textsf{michaels} then loses its pass,
with the two mean families moving $0.050 \to 0.186$ and
$0.107 \to 0.202$. The offset model therefore has to be chosen per
rig, and the choice needs no refit of the dynamics.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "Round 4", "Round 5", "Conclusion"

\subsubsection{A distribution over rigs}
\label{sec:traj-post}
Seven rigs is not enough to learn a 32-dimensional density, so the
rig hyperprior is deliberately the simplest thing that can be sampled:
a diagonal Gaussian. What makes it defensible is the
reparametrization. Every coordinate is made dimensionless before the
Gaussian is fitted: one scale coordinate $\log\overline{\mu}$; three
relative trims (roll, pitch and yaw as a fraction of the hover level);
the already dimensionless $\beta$, $\log f_0$, $\mathrm{logit}\,\zeta$
and $\log\tau_{\mathrm e}$; and every $\sigma$ as
$\log(\sigma/\overline\mu)$, a relative fluctuation. A draw is then
``a drone this big, fluctuating this much relative to its size'',
which matters because the seven rigs differ in absolute size by
$3.6\times$: a Gaussian over raw parameters would mostly encode how
big the drone is, and a draw combining one rig's hover level with
another's absolute jitter would be nonsense. Sampling maps back
through the same transform, so $\mu > 0$, the bounded parameters stay
in their ranges and $\tau_{\mathrm s}$ stays above $1/(2\pi f_0)$ by
construction. Each of the seven rigs sits within 1.51--2.38 standard
deviations of the fitted Gaussian on its informative coordinates.
% source: results/rps_traj/posterior.json, via docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md "Rig posterior"

One detail is load-bearing. A rig with no between-flight level
difference has $s = 0$, which the log coordinate must write as a
floor; averaging those floors in dragged that coordinate's mean to
$-5.7$ with a standard deviation of 3.9, and a $+2\sigma$ draw then
asked for a per-flight offset eight times the hover level. A floored
zero is a different fact from a small value, so rigs without the
information are left out of that coordinate's moments. This is a
sampler and not a population estimate: it is fitted on seven rigs, six
of them one airframe with one controller tune, and the diagonal
Gaussian has no covariance structure between coordinates that the rigs
demonstrably share.
% source: docs/experiments/rps-trajectory-model.md, "Rig posterior"

\subsection{Rotor noise}
\label{sec:noise}

Given the carrier $\mathbf r(t)$ --- a window-refined constant on a
static bench, a trajectory in flight --- the microphone signal is a
sum of lines plus a floor,
\begin{equation}
  x_m(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{4}\sum_{k=1}^{K_i} A_{mik}(t)\cos\phi_{mik}(t)
    \;+\; n_m(t),
  \label{eq:noisegen}
\end{equation}
with the phase of line $(i,k)$ at microphone $m$
\begin{equation}
  \phi_{mik}(t) = 2\pi k\!\int_0^t\! r_i(s)\,\mathrm ds
    \;+\; k\,\theta_i(t) \;+\; \psi_{ik}(t) \;+\; \alpha_{mik}.
  \label{eq:phase}
\end{equation}
The three stochastic terms are the model's content.
% source: docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Model R3: Generation"

\subsubsection{Shaft}
One process per rotor, shared by all its orders
and all microphones: an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck speed error $\nu_i$ in
rad/s integrated into an angle error,
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm d\nu_i = -\lambda\nu_i\,\mathrm dt
    + \sqrt{2\lambda}\,\sigma_\nu\,\mathrm dW_i,
  \qquad \mathrm d\theta_i = \nu_i\,\mathrm dt,
  \label{eq:shaft}
\end{equation}
started stationary. Its increment variance is
$V_\theta(\tau) = 2\sigma_\nu^2[\,|\tau|/\lambda - (1 -
e^{-\lambda|\tau|})/\lambda^2\,]$. Because the term enters the phase
multiplied by $k$, it broadens order $k$ as $k^2$, which is how it is
separated from the next term.
% source: docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Model R3: Generation"

\subsubsection{Per-line width}
One Wiener phase per rotor and order,
independent across $(i,k)$ and shared across microphones,
$\mathrm d\psi_{ik} = \sqrt{4\pi\gamma_{ik}}\,\mathrm dW_{ik}$, so that
$\mathbb E\,e^{\mathrm i\Delta\psi} = e^{-2\pi\gamma_{ik}|\tau|}$ and
the line is a Lorentzian of half width $\gamma_{ik}$ in Hz. There is
no law across $k$: each $\gamma_{ik}$ is a free non-negative number.
This replaced a shared per-order Ornstein--Uhlenbeck pair in an
earlier version of the model, which was over-parametrized in exactly
one place --- a 128 ms flight window identifies only the product of
its two parameters, and the profiled objective was flat to 0.03
nats per cell over three decades of the rate.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round1/basin/findings.md, via docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd "Proposed after rounds 1--2"

\subsubsection{Amplitude, profile and speed law}
With
$P_{ik} = 10^{p_{ik}/10}$ the line power of order $k$ of rotor $i$ and
$p_{ik}$ in dB the \emph{profile},
\begin{equation}
  A_{mik}(t) = \sqrt{2P_{ik}}
    \Bigl(\tfrac{r_i(t)}{r_{\mathrm{ref}}}\Bigr)^{a/2}
    10^{(g_{mi} - \bar g_{\cdot i})/20}\;
    10^{(G_m - \bar G)/20},
  \label{eq:amp}
\end{equation}
where $a$ is the comb's speed exponent, $g_{mi}$ the per-microphone
line gain of rotor $i$ and $G_m$ the per-microphone overall gain, both
mean-pinned over microphones so that they carry no absolute level.
These two gain sets are the model's microphone pattern: they are what
makes an eight-channel render differ channel to channel, and they are
fitted, not assumed. On a static bench $a = 0$, the speed being one
constant absorbed by $p_{ik}$. When a comb fitted on the bench is
transplanted into a flight fit, one extra scalar $c$ in dB is added to
every $p_{ik}$ --- the level of a transplanted comb, and the only
absolute scale it has. $\alpha_{mik}$ is a fixed uniform phase per
$(m,i,k)$, so components add in power.
% source: docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Model R3: Generation"

\subsubsection{Floor}
The floor is white noise per microphone shaped by
the square root of
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  S_m(f,t) &= 10^{h_m/10}
    \Bigl[\tfrac14\textstyle\sum_i
      \bigl(r_i(t)/r_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr)^{b} + s\Bigr]\,
    10^{\Sigma_F(f)/10},\\
  \Sigma_F(f) &= \mu_F + \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{14}
    B_j(f)\,\sigma_B\,(\mathbf L\mathbf z)_j + t_F\log_2(f/f_t),
\end{aligned}
  \label{eq:floor}
\end{equation}
with $\mu_F$ the floor level in dB, $\mathbf z$ the 14 standard-normal
control-point coordinates of a Gaussian-process-interpolated spectral
shape ($\mathbf L$ its Cholesky factor, $B_j$ the interpolation basis
on a log-frequency grid, $\sigma_B$ a fixed shape scale), $t_F$ a tilt
in dB/octave about $f_t$, $b$ the floor's speed exponent, $s$ its
static fraction and $h_m$ the per-microphone floor gain. The two speed
laws $a$ and $b$ and the static fraction $s$ exist only in flight;
they are what lets one fitted rig cover standby, ramp and cruise.
Everything is synthesized on a 64 kHz work grid, anti-aliased and
decimated to 16 kHz, and the fit sees the same chain as a fixed power
transfer $\mathcal T(f)$.
% source: docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Model R3: Generation"

\subsubsection{Regimes}
A rotor at standby and the same rotor at
cruise are not one comb at two speeds: the blade-passing structure,
the parity of the loud orders and the floor all change. One rig may
therefore carry two fitted parameter sets, a \emph{standby} one and a
\emph{cruise} one, and the renderer interpolates their line and floor
powers by a smoothstep in the mean carrier, holding the standby set
below 45\revps{} and the cruise set above 65\revps{}. Where a rig has
no standby recording, its standby slot is empty and the cruise set is
used throughout.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round3/fits/findings_regimes.md

\subsection{Fitting the rotor-noise model}
\label{sec:fit}

\subsubsection{Objective}
A \emph{support} is a set of frames $q$ of one
recording: on the bench, one frame covering the whole stationary
window (12--34 s, one periodogram); in flight, periodic-Hann frames of
$N = 2048$ at hop 512 and 16 kHz, i.e. $T = 128$ ms, pooled over
windows. The observation is the periodogram $I_{mqf}$ on the band
$30 \le f \le \min(7900,\,0.45 f_{\mathrm s})$ Hz. Under the model its
expectation is, with $w_{\mathrm{acf}}$ the window's autocorrelation
and $\bar r_{iq}$ the mean carrier of rotor $i$ in frame $q$,
\begin{align}
  \Lambda_{mqf} &= \mathcal T(f)\,10^{(G_m - \bar G)/10}
    \Bigl[\sum_i 10^{(g_{mi} - \bar g_{\cdot i})/10}\,
      \Lambda^{\mathrm{line}}_{iqf} \nonumber\\
  &\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad + 10^{h_m/10}\,
      \Lambda^{\mathrm{floor}}_{qf}\Bigr],
  \label{eq:expper}\\
  \Lambda^{\mathrm{line}}_{iqf} &= \frac{1}{\sum_n w_n^2}
    \sum_{|\tau| < T} w_{\mathrm{acf}}(\tau)\,e^{-2\pi \mathrm i f\tau}
    \nonumber\\
  &\quad\times \sum_k P_{ik}
    \Bigl(\tfrac{\bar r_{iq}}{r_{\mathrm{ref}}}\Bigr)^{a}
    \rho_{ik}(\tau)\cos\bigl(2\pi k \bar r_{iq}\tau\bigr),
  \label{eq:linespec}
\end{align}
where the coherence of line $(i,k)$ collects the two phase noises,
\begin{equation}
  \rho_{ik}(\tau) = \exp\Bigl[-\tfrac{k^2}{2}V_\theta(\tau)
    - 2\pi\gamma_{ik}|\tau|\Bigr].
  \label{eq:coh}
\end{equation}
In flight the atom follows the label's trajectory inside the frame, so
it is a chirped rather than a stationary atom. Lines and floor are
independent, so their expected periodograms add. The fit objective is
the composite Whittle risk with a MAP prior,
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L(\Theta) = \sum_q w_q \sum_m \sum_{f}
    \Bigl[\frac{I_{mqf}}{\Lambda_{mqf}}
      + \log \Lambda_{mqf}\Bigr] - \log p(\Theta),
  \label{eq:whittle}
\end{equation}
with $\Lambda$ evaluated at $\Theta$, the sum over $f$ running over
the band, and $w_q$ exposure weights that normalise overlapping frames
per unique second. Below 300 Hz the floor dominates the risk and above it
the comb; we report the two bands separately throughout, and the comb
band is the decisive one.
% source: docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Model R3: Likelihood"

\subsubsection{Two stages}
The dynamics are fitted on a static bench
and not in flight, because the flight labels are not good enough to
carry them: at order $k = 70$ the free-flight telemetry disagrees with
the audio by about 1 Hz of standard deviation, which is the whole
quantity a line width is supposed to measure. Stage one fits each
DREGON rotor separately on single-motor bench recordings at 50--90
rev/s with everything free --- $\sigma_\nu$, $\lambda$, the
$\gamma_{ik}$ ladder, the profile, the floor and the microphone gains
--- at $k_{\max}$ between 89 and 130. Stage two fits the flight, with
the dynamics frozen at the log-means of the four bench fits
($\sigma_\nu = 0.742318$ rad/s, $\lambda = 0.060800$ s$^{-1}$; rotor
$i$ takes motor $i$'s width ladder) and the per-order profile, the
floor and the microphone gains free, at $k_{\max} = 88$.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/fits/findings.md;
% docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Fit blocks per mode"

The fit runs 1500 Adam steps at learning rate 0.02 and batch 8,
then 300 L-BFGS steps on a deterministic 64-frame subset, from four
starts: one data-driven and three log-normal perturbations of it, with
the lowest polished objective reported. Convergence is declared when
the restart gain falls below $10^{-4}$ nats per cell. \emph{No fit in
this campaign converged by that test}: the R5 flight fit's restart
gain is $1.7$--$2.5\times10^{-3}$ nats per cell. What the restarts do
agree on is the answer. The four starts return Whittle risks of
$-8.712373$, $-8.712293$, $-8.712558$ and $-8.712450$ nats per cell
--- a best-to-worst spread of $1.9\times10^{-4}$ --- and the frozen
dynamics are bit-identical across them. The flight fit improves on the
previous round's on the same 2\,056\,320 cells, $-8.5931 \to -8.7124$
nats per cell.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/fits/findings.md

\subsubsection{Priors and the speed-span pin}
The priors are measured
rather than chosen, and Appendix~\ref{sec:fittables} lists them with
their derivations. Two matter for reading the results. The line widths
take $\gamma_{ik}\sim\mathrm{LN}(0.01k\ \mathrm{Hz}, 1.0)$, anchored on
the bench decoherence law $V_\psi \approx 0.09\,k^{1.1}\tau^{0.43}$
rad$^2$, i.e. an effective diffusion of about $0.1k$ rad$^2$/s; one
log standard deviation is a factor 2.7, so a line may be seven times
wider or narrower than that law at $2\sigma$ but cannot absorb the
shaft core.
% source: docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Parameters, with their priors"

The second is the \emph{speed-span pin}. The three flight-only
parameters $a$, $b$ and $s$ are identified only by the range of speeds
in the fitting pool, and a cruise-only pool has almost none. When the
pool's carrier span $\max/\min$ falls below $1.5\times$, all three are
pinned at their prior medians ($a = 2$, $b = 2$,
$s = 2.5\times10^{-3}$) and the fit records which were pinned. The
rule exists because of what happens without it: on a DREGON cruise
pool of span $1.14\times$ the floor exponent ran to 38.8 and the
static fraction to 17 --- four standard deviations out --- putting the
standby floor about 37 dB above the real clip, and an earlier
cruise-only fit took $a = 10.02$. A pooled fit spanning $4.68\times$
pins nothing. The rule is a threshold and not a cure: the R5 flight
pool spans $1.743918\times$, just above the threshold, so nothing was
pinned and the fit returned $a = -0.868132$ (the comb getting
\emph{quieter} with speed) and $b = 15.321160$. We do not report those
two as measurements, and Section~\ref{sec:rigs} pins them at the prior
medians in every sampled rig.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/fits/findings.md;
% results/noise_v2/rounds/round3/fits/findings_regimes.md

\subsubsection{What is identified}
A basin scan around a converged
cruise fit, holding every block but one and sweeping over two decades,
separates the two. $\sigma_\nu$ has leverage 1.9968 nats per cell and
is identified. The shaft rate $\lambda$ is not: the profiled objective
is flat to 0.0307 nats per cell over 2.86 decades, because a 128 ms
lag cannot see it. That is why $\lambda$ is fitted on the bench, where
the window is 30 s, and frozen in flight. Within a rotor, low orders
return the resolution floor for $\gamma_{ik}$ and their shape is the
shaft's alone, which pins $\sigma_\nu$; at high orders whatever
exceeds the $k^2$ shaft prediction is $\gamma_{ik}$. One degeneracy is
possible and is tested after every bench fit rather than assumed away:
in the Brownian limit the shaft term is also Lorentzian and a free
$\gamma_{ik} \propto k^2$ could absorb it, so the fit passes only if
the fitted widths at $k \le 4$ sit at the resolution floor.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round1/basin/findings.md;
% docs/explainers/noise-model-v2-plan.qmd, "Identification, and the check that goes with it"

\subsection{Validating the fits}
\label{sec:fitval}

A fitted generative model is validated by what it is for. We use three
instruments, in decreasing order of authority.

\subsubsection{Tracker parity}
The decisive one asks whether a
rotor-speed estimator trained on real audio, frozen, reads the render
as well as it reads a recording. We use an HPPNet with the per-rotor
output representation of Section~\ref{sec:est}, trained on the real
pool and checkpoint-pinned by hash so that scoring dies on a mismatch,
and we score the permutation-invariant MAE over all eight microphones
and four frozen render seeds on five 4-s cruise windows per rig,
aggregating per recording. The bar is parity with the previous
generation of synthetic arms: 2.187786\revps{} on DREGON, where the
same tracker reads the real audio at 1.218708, and $1.05\times$
3.026661 on the Matrice 100.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/score/findings.md

The fitted model reads 1.820065\revps{} on DREGON, a margin of
$+0.368$ over the parity bar, and 1.621670\revps{} on the Matrice 100,
a margin of $+1.556$. Per DREGON recording the renders score
1.423033 (free flight), 1.648841 (hovering), 1.931465 (up/down),
2.364579 (rectangle) and 1.732407 (spinning), against 0.638129,
0.888408, 1.694930, 1.685142 and 1.186931 for the real recordings; so
two of the five renders are already read as well as the real audio and
three are not. A stretch bar at 70\,\% of the way from the bar to the
real audio, 1.897063, is passed on the mean by $+0.077$ but not by the
one-sided 95\,\% upper bound over recordings, 2.158331. The
progression over the campaign is the reason to trust the number more
than any single comparison: on the same protocol the DREGON renders
scored 78.80, 72.34 and 71.87\revps{} in the three previous rounds.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/score/findings.md;
% results/noise_v2/rounds/round3/score/findings.md

\subsubsection{Spectral proxy and oracle likelihood}
The second
instrument is the absolute difference in long-term average spectrum
between the render and the real recording at microphone 0, per
support. It is a proxy and it fails, narrowly: 2.0298 dB on DREGON
against a gate of 1.9786 dB and 1.2816 dB on the Matrice 100 against
1.2197 dB, i.e. short by 0.05 and 0.06 dB. It has improved from 3.7518
dB over the campaign. The third asks how much likelihood the fitted
model leaves on the table against a speed-matched stationary oracle,
i.e. an empirical spectrum measured at the same carriers. On the
decisive comb band the fitted model scores $-373\,666.30$ nats/s
against the oracle's $-371\,916.50$, a margin of $-1749.80$ nats/s,
which passes the frozen convention; on the floor band the model is
better than the oracle by 368.04 nats/s, which we report but do not
read as an achievement.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/score/findings.md

\todo{Fig.~3: fitted expected periodogram against the real
  periodogram, one DREGON cruise support and one FLY125 cruise
  support, comb band and floor band.}

\subsubsection{What the tracker gate actually measures}
The gate is
sharper than a distance, and a probe of an earlier fit shows why. That
fit scored 69.555\revps{} under the same HPPNet, which looks like
total mistracking and is not: the tracker emits exactly 0\revps{} on
86.3\,\% of the scored values, i.e. it puts the render in the zero
class it was trained to recognize as ``rotors stopped''. Per
microphone the errors are 80.37\revps{} on five channels and 10.23 and
4.37 on two others, against a mean carrier of 80.39: the tracker
either reads the comb or does not see it. A regressor trained on the
same pool collapses on exactly one of the eight channels (per-channel
79.82, 1.69, 0.77, 0.78, 2.15, 0.89, 3.05, 0.99), and its aggregate of
11.297 is that one dead channel. The broadband level is not the
explanation: that render is 3--7 dB down per channel, but the dying
channel is not the quietest. What separates the arms is the carrier
gain in the tracker's own front end --- the prominence of the true
comb against mis-tuned combs at its 855 ms, $Q = 68.75$ analysis ---
which reads $+1.63$ dB on the failing render against $+5.57$ to
$+5.98$ dB on the arms the tracker reads. The gate therefore measures
whether the fitted comb clears the estimator's detection boundary, not
whether the render resembles the recording in any average sense, and
that is exactly the property a training pool needs.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/tracker_probe/findings.md

Two caveats go with it. First, the boundary is sufficient and not
necessary: the \emph{real} clip's own carrier gain is $+0.98$ dB, well
below the threshold, and it is tracked anyway at 1.074\revps{}. A
render that clears the boundary is safe, but one that does not is not
thereby refuted. Second, and more important for reading the reference
numbers in Section~\ref{sec:exp}: the frozen trackers were trained on
a pool that is 83.3\,\% real recordings and 16.7\,\% zero-labelled
silence, with no synthetic rig renders in it at all, but the DREGON
split they use excludes only one of the room-1 recordings, so all
three of the recordings scored here are inside the trackers' own
training pool. The real-audio anchors of 1.074 and 1.614\revps{} are
therefore in-domain numbers on seen recordings, and the gate's margin
should be read against the synthetic bar, which is not.
% source: results/noise_v2/rounds/round5/tracker_probe/findings.md

\subsection{Sampling rigs}
\label{sec:rigs}

A fit is one aircraft. Training on it is training on a point, and a
point is what the previous generation of experiments showed to be the
limit: a model trained on two fitted rigs as fixed parameter vectors
overfits them and transfers unevenly. We therefore draw rigs from the
fits in three ways, of increasing distance from the measured
aircraft.

\textbf{Neighbourhood} (the \emph{easy} bank, 1024 entries per rig).
Each entry is a perturbation of one measured rig. The harmonic profile
of each rotor is decomposed as
$p_{ik} = \mathrm{gain}_i + \mathrm{slope}_i(\log_{10}k -
\overline{\log_{10}k}) + \mathrm{resid}_i(k)$; the gain and the slope
are perturbed and the residual is partially redrawn from a
squared-exponential kernel in log order, mixed rather than added so
that the fine-structure variance stays at the anchor's. The line
widths and the shaft pair $(\sigma_\nu,\lambda)$ move in log space,
the floor moves through its level, its tilt, an AR(1) perturbation of
its Gaussian-process coordinates and its per-microphone gains, and the
channel structure moves through $g_{mi}$ and $G_m$. The widths of all
of these at strength 1 are \emph{measured}: they are the
between-restart spread of the fits themselves, so the cloud is at
least as wide as our own uncertainty about the aircraft, and strength
is a single multiplier on all of them chosen so that the cloud
brackets the real clip in at least 90\,\% of the 1/3-octave bands
above 300 Hz, per rig. Each entry keeps the trajectory law of the rig
it came from, so a DREGON comb is never flown on a Matrice 100
envelope.

\textbf{Path} (the \emph{hard} bank, 2048 entries). A mixing
coordinate $t\sim U[0,1]$ interpolates the two measured rigs'
\emph{cruise} fits in the same decomposed coordinates, on their common
order range $k = 1,\ldots,81$; DREGON's orders 82--88 are dropped and
the drop is recorded in the entry's provenance. The neighbourhood
perturbation is then applied around that interpolated point. Standby
is never interpolated --- a standby comb is a different regime, not a
slower cruise --- so the standby slot is carried as a policy: at
mixing coordinate $t$ the entry takes the Matrice 100's fitted standby
fit with probability $t$ and no standby fit otherwise, which makes a
Matrice-like draw usually two-regime and a DREGON-like draw usually
single-regime. Rigs resembling either real aircraft therefore exist
but neither is privileged, so no fingerprint can be memorized.

\textbf{Hyperprior}. The trajectory half of a hard entry is left
unbound and drawn from the diagonal Gaussian over rigs of
Section~\ref{sec:traj-post}, rig-balanced. This is the only part of
the pipeline that produces an airframe no dataset contains, and it is
why the hard arm is hard on both halves at once.

The hyperprior is used under one documented truncation. The salience
architectures of Section~\ref{sec:est} have a fixed speed grid that
ends at 150\revps, so a sampled flight whose fastest rotor exceeds
that is rejected and redrawn whole, never clipped; the streams
therefore train on the hyperprior conditioned on
$\max_i \max_t r_i(t) \le 150$\revps. The acceptance rate is 0.296.
The cost is hover level and not rig diversity: the log hover-scale
coordinate shifts hard (mean $4.971 \to 4.406$, standard deviation
$0.497 \to 0.275$, $z = -33.2$), while all 31 remaining shape and
dynamics coordinates of the scale-free rig vector are statistically
unmoved (largest $|z|$ is 1.71 and every accepted-to-all standard
deviation ratio lies in 0.951--1.031). The surviving hover levels have
median 86.1, 90th percentile 111.9 and maximum 182.0\revps, against
144.2, 274.5 and 613.6 uncapped.
% source: docs/experiments/noise-v2-transfer.md;
% src/data_processing/trajectory_model/source.py (rps_max)

Guards reject and redraw rather than clip, and all of them are
structural rather than cosmetic: the expected periodogram must be
finite and positive at cruise (80\revps) \emph{and} at idle
(30\revps); each rotor's profile trend must still fall with order by
at least 3 dB over the fitted range; the total line-width excursion is
capped at $1.5\times$; the draw's expected periodogram must lie within
twice the measured real clip-to-clip band RMS of that rig's own
validation windows in the 1/3-octave bands from 300 to 7900 Hz; and
negative speed exponents are refused.

Every entry in both banks carries the short-span contract of
Section~\ref{sec:fit}: $a = 2$, $b = 2$ and $s = 2.5\times10^{-3}$,
the prior medians, recorded per entry, because a cruise-only pool
cannot identify them. The cruise profile is left at its fitted
80\revps{} reference and the trajectories keep their own speed labels;
there is no hover rescaling. Both banks are built by one script from a
single seed and are bit-reproducible.
% source: scripts/noise_v2_build_bank.py; conf/online_mix/noise_v2_easy_5050.yaml,
% conf/online_mix/noise_v2_hard_5050.yaml

The per-rotor dynamics block is therefore $2 + K_i$ parameters. The
$\gamma_{ik}$ prior is anchored on the bench decoherence law and the
$p_{ik}$ prior on each line's measured level, which lands the
data-driven start within 0.4--1.5 dB of the fitted value; parking
invisible orders at a wide zero-mean prior instead produced a 400 Hz
pedestal above the floor in an earlier round.
